newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa goes for economic gold with Olympics bid.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa goes for economic gold with Olympics bid.

text.p: South Africa, shortlisted on Friday to host the continent's first Olympic Games, will win a lasting economic prize if it secures the event, business leaders and analysts said.

Capital spending of 7.5 billion rand ($1.7 billion) on the Games should help revive a flagging economy, creating tens of thousands of badly needed jobs and boosting earnings of construction, engineering, hotels and other companies.
The Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) estimates a successful bid would inject 30 billion rand into the economy between 1997 and 2006 and generate more than 90,000 permanent jobs.
"It will have a very significant impact, particularly on the greater Cape Town area," said Colin Boyes, deputy director of the Cape Chamber of Commerce.
"The Games will give us a badly needed upgrade of our infrastructure while the momentum of the tourist industry -- in many ways Cape gold -- should be carried forward a lot faster."

But the gains will not be limited only to the Western Cape province, already South Africa's most dynamic region with a growth rate 1.5 to 2.0 percentage points ahead of the three percent national average.

Given the region's reliance on goods from the industrial heartland of Gauteng, around Johannesburg and Pretoria, the DBSA estimates that 60 percent of the economic impact will actually be felt in other provinces.
"Every time there is an increase in activity in Cape Town, there is an increase elsewhere, mostly in Gauteng," said Chris Ball, the bid's executive officer.
Some economists forecast the Games could lift overall growth in South Africa by one percentage point over the next 10 years.
For investors picking the right stocks there could be handsome returns, according to David Sylvester of stockbrokers TA Securities.
"I think it is something investors on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange will focus on, once we get the final go-ahead and things start happening on the ground," he ground.

Stock market "gold medal" winners could include construction and property companies like Stocks and Stocks, Group Five and Basil Read ; shipping concerns such as Safmarine & Rennies Holdings and Griffin Shipping; and, of course, beer producer South African Breweries.
Another big winner is likely to be Telkom, the state-owned telecommunications concern 30 percent of which is about to be sold to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium in a landmark privatisation deal.
Of the overall capital budget, some five billion rand would be spent on venues, housing and bulk services and 2.6 billion on indirect investment including transport upgrades.
Central and local government plan to fund 55 percent of the total with the private sector contributing 35 percent and 10 percent coming from the Olympic committee.
The International Olympic Committee also shortlisted Rome, Athens, Buenos Aires and Stockholm as final candidates to host the 2004 Summer Games on Friday.
The cities, chosen from 11 candidates, will now go forward to a vote of the full IOC session on September 5 when the venue for the Games will be decided.
